planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep and 8-10 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun, giving each bulb room to display its broad foliage.

directions: Red Giant is a selection of the species Turkestan onion chosen for its broad, wavy-edged leaves that emerge flushed with maroon-purple before fading to gray-green, a richer coloring than the plain species offers. In mid-to-late spring a short, stout stalk barely clears the foliage to open a dense, basketball-sized umbel of reddish-purple starry florets that holds its shape for weeks and dries well for arrangements. Its low, broad habit is strikingly different from taller, leafless-stemmed ornamental onions, making it a good front-of-border or rock garden accent. The foliage yellows and dies back shortly after bloom, so interplant with later-emerging perennials to mask the fading leaves.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this compact Chinese species was introduced to Western gardens by plant collector Reginald Farrer and increases steadily into dense clumps.

directions: Farrer's onion forms a tidy clump of narrow, strap-shaped leaves topped in early to midsummer by loose, one-sided clusters of nodding, bell-shaped flowers in a deep reddish-violet, quite distinct from the tight, upward-facing globes of most ornamental onions. Its relaxed, arching flower stems and rich color make it a good choice for the front of a border, a rock garden, or massed as a small-scale ground accent beneath taller perennials. It prefers soil that does not dry out completely during the growing season, unlike many summer-dormant alliums from drier habitats. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigorous flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs or divisions in fall or early spring in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to part shade; this compact selection flowers later and more profusely than the species, continuing into the first light frosts.

directions: Ozawa is a dwarf, especially floriferous selection of the autumn-blooming Japanese onion, forming a low mound of narrow, grass-like leaves that stays more compact and dense than the straight species. In September and October it produces an abundance of rounded, rosy-purple to magenta flower heads that are notably larger and more numerous than those of the species, opening when few other bulbs are in flower. As the display finishes, the foliage turns a showy tawny orange, adding a second season of interest before winter dormancy. Its low, tidy habit suits edging, rock gardens, and the front of a fall-interest border; clumps increase slowly and can be divided in spring every three to four years.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2 inches deep in fall in well-drained, rocky to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; this selected form flowers somewhat earlier and more showily than wild nodding onion.

directions: Hidcote is a selected form of the North American native nodding onion chosen for flower heads that are larger, darker, and earlier-opening than those of the wild species. In early to midsummer the curved, pendant stalks carry dense clusters of rich magenta-rose, bell-shaped florets that hang gracefully below the slender foliage, a striking improvement in color saturation over the pink-to-white species. It thrives in the same poor, dry, rocky soils that satisfy the species and is equally valuable for pollinators, drawing native bees and butterflies through its bloom period. Outstanding in rock gardens, dry meadow plantings, and native borders; it self-seeds moderately and can be divided in fall if clumps become crowded.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown starts into well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to dappled shade; this diminutive South African species is excellent for a warm rock garden or container where its evening fragrance can be enjoyed up close.

directions: Natal pink wild garlic is the smallest commonly grown Tulbaghia, forming tight, slowly spreading clumps of narrow, semi-evergreen foliage well suited to a trough, rock garden, or warm container planting. From late spring into summer it produces dainty umbels of muted lavender-pink flowers with a contrasting yellow-green crown at the center of each bloom, opening a sweet, clove-like fragrance that intensifies in the afternoon and evening. Unlike Society Garlic, its foliage carries little garlic odor, making it a pleasant choice for planting near seating areas and pathways. It is deciduous in hard freezes but resprouts reliably from the rootstock where winters stay above the mid-teens.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2 inches deep and 3 inches apart in sharply well-drained, lean soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; this dwarf form stays only a few inches tall and suits a trough, crevice garden, or the front edge of a gravel bed.

directions: Nanum is a miniature form of yellow allium, reduced to only a few inches in height while keeping the same loose, airy flower heads as the species. In midsummer slender stems barely rise above the thread-like, blue-green foliage to open small clusters of pendant, lemon-yellow, bell-shaped florets on uneven stalks, giving an open, spraying look rather than a tight globe. Its tiny stature makes it easy to lose in a mixed border, so it is best reserved for rock gardens, raised troughs, crevice plantings, or pots where it can be appreciated up close. Like the species it demands sharp drainage and resents rich, moist soil, which encourages weak growth and poor flowering.
